pages.summary: A transfer function model: a ratio of polynomials in s (or z).
body: The numerator and denominator are coefficients in descending powers, continuous unless a sample time is given; cells of them make a model with several inputs and outputs. `s = tf('s')` lets a model be written as an expression. Models add, subtract, multiply (`sys1*sys2` feeds sys2 into sys1), divide, invert, raise to powers, concatenate and index; the result keeps the most general kind. Every analysis and response function takes them.
syntax: The Laplace variable, to write models with.
Another model as a transfer function.

pages.summary: A model as its zeros, poles and gain.
body: Shown as products of first-order factors (second-order for complex pairs), which reads off where the poles and zeros are. Any model can be turned into this form; `Z`, `P` and `K` hold them.
syntax: The variable, to write models with.

pages.summary: A state-space model: x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du.
body: Matrices A, B, C and D (in discrete time x(k+1) = Ax(k) + Bu(k)); a static gain from D alone. A transfer function becomes a realization of it (the controller canonical form); `'minimal'` drops states that cannot be controlled or observed. Properties A, B, C, D and the states' names.
syntax: sys = ss(A, B, C, D, Ts)

pages.summary: PID controllers, made and tuned for a plant.
body: `pid` makes Kp + Ki/s + Kd s/(Tf s + 1) (missing gains 0); its gains read and set as properties, and it works as its transfer function everywhere. `pidtune` designs a controller of a type (P, I, PI by default, PD, PID, PDF, PIDF) for a plant: the loop crosses over at a frequency (chosen, or given) with the phase margin `pidtuneOptions` sets (60 degrees). PyLAB's own design rules.
syntax: At a crossover, with options; and what it achieved.

examples.title: A slow plant, a PI controller tuned for it

pages.summary: Models joined: in a loop, side by side with their outputs added, and side by side apart.
body: `feedback(sys1, sys2)` closes a loop with sys1 forward and sys2 back: sys1/(1 + sys2 sys1) for negative feedback, or positive with sign +1. `parallel` adds two models' outputs; `series` (on its own page) chains them. `append` puts models side by side, unconnected: a block-diagonal model.

examples.title: A loop closed around an integrator
examples.code:
G = tf(2, [1 3 0]);
T = feedback(G, 1)
P = parallel(tf(1, [1 1]), tf(1, [1 2]))
size(append(G, P, 5))

pages.summary: Models joined by the names of their signals.
body: `sumblk` makes a summing junction from a formula such as `'e = r - y'`, its input and output names those of the formula. `connect` joins models by name: each input is driven by the output of the same name, or is one of the inputs named; the outputs named are the result's. A loop of several blocks is written as it is drawn.

examples.title: A loop by names

pages.summary: A model's data in each form, and conversions of the matrices.
body: `tfdata`, `zpkdata` and `ssdata` give a model's numerators and denominators, zeros, poles and gains, or state matrices (as cells, or rows with `'v'` for one input and output). `ss2tf` and `tf2ss` convert between state matrices and transfer function coefficients directly.
syntax: [b, a] = ss2tf(A, B, C, D, iu)

examples.title: One model, its data three ways

pages.summary: A model's poles and zeros, and their map.
body: The poles are where the response grows or decays (the eigenvalues of A, the denominator's roots); the zeros where the response vanishes. `tzero` gives the transmission zeros of a model with several inputs and outputs, where its system matrix loses rank. `pzmap` draws poles (x) and zeros (o) in the complex plane.

examples.title: A lightly damped system with a zero
examples.code:
G = tf([1 0.5], conv([1 0.4 4], [1 2]));
pole(G).'
zero(G)
pzmap(G), grid on

pages.summary: A model's gain: at rest, at one frequency, and over many.
body: `dcgain` gives the steady-state gain, H(0) (H(1) in discrete time). `evalfr` gives the response at one complex frequency; `freqresp` at frequencies in rad/s (on the unit circle, e^(jwTs), in discrete time), as an ny-by-nu-by-n array.

examples.title: A first-order lag

pages.summary: The natural frequencies and damping of a model's poles, and whether it is stable.
body: For each pole, its natural frequency |p| and damping ratio -cos(angle(p)) (from log(p)/Ts in discrete time), in order of frequency; with no output a table with the time constants. A model is stable when every pole has a negative real part (lies inside the unit circle in discrete time).
syntax: The frequencies, damping ratios and poles.

pages.summary: Continuous models made discrete, discrete made continuous, and resampled.
body: `c2d` discretizes at a sample time: `'zoh'` (exact for inputs held between samples, the default), `'foh'`, `'tustin'`, `'matched'` or `'impulse'`. `d2c` goes back (by the matrix logarithm, or the inverse bilinear map); `d2d` resamples a discrete model through the continuous one.

pages.summary: A delay approximated by a ratio of polynomials.
body: exp(-sT) as a ratio of polynomials of degree N whose numerator is the denominator at -s: its gain is exactly 1 at every frequency, its phase right at low frequencies. `pade(sys, N)` replaces a model's delays by their approximations, so that analyses needing polynomials can take it.

examples.title: One second of delay

body: `minreal` takes out what cancels: coinciding poles and zeros of a transfer function, or states that cannot be controlled or observed. `ss2ss` transforms the states (z = Tx), `xperm` reorders them, and `canon` gives the modal form (A block diagonal, real 2-by-2 blocks for complex pairs) or the companion form. The input-output behaviour stays the same.

pages.summary: Responses in time: to a step, from initial conditions, and to any input.
body: `step` gives (or draws) the response to a unit step, long enough for the slowest pole to settle unless a time is given, as a staircase in discrete time; several models are drawn together. `initial` gives the response of a state-space model from an initial state with no input; `lsim` the response to an input sampled at times (linear between samples, unless `'zoh'`). `stepplot` and `impulseplot` draw them.
syntax: [y, t, x] = lsim(sys, u, t, x0)

examples.title: A square wave through a lag, and a release from rest

pages.summary: Characteristics of a response: rise and settling times, overshoot, peak.
body: `stepinfo` gives a step response's rise time (10% to 90% of the change), settling time (within 2% of the final value), overshoot and undershoot in percent, and the peak and its time, from a model or from samples. `lsiminfo` gives a response's settling time and its minimum and maximum with their times.
syntax: S = stepinfo(y, t, yfinal, 'SettlingTimeThreshold', s, 'RiseTimeLimits', [lo hi])
